1065: How many glucoses does the transferred tree carry?
1067: A second glucose leaves. With a single glucose left, the protein is taken in charge by chaperones that help it fold.
1068: Glucosidase II removes the two α1-3-linked glucoses. The monoglucosylated form is the ligand of the lectins calnexin (membrane-bound) and calreticulin (soluble), associated with the disulfide isomerase ERp57.
1073: α-Glucosidase II, then UGGT1 if needed
1074: The last glucose is removed: the protein is released. If it is misfolded, an enzyme puts a glucose back, and it returns to the chaperones.
1075: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase (UGGT1) is the folding sensor: it only reglucosylates proteins exposing hydrophobic surfaces. This back-and-forth is the calnexin/calreticulin cycle.
1080: A clock is ticking: a slow mannosidase removes one mannose. If well folded, the protein leaves for the Golgi; otherwise more mannoses will be removed and it will be destroyed.
1081: MAN1B1 removes the terminal mannose of branch B. EDEM proteins then remove those of branch C: the α1-6 mannose thus exposed is read by OS-9, which delivers the protein to the HRD1/SEL1L complex for retrotranslocation and degradation by the proteasome (ERAD).
1082: Which signal sends a glycoprotein to ERAD?
1087: The reticulum is an oxidising environment, unlike the cytosol: the cysteines of secreted proteins are linked there by bonds that lock their fold.
1088: One disulfide bond formed, one H₂O₂ molecule produced: oxidative folding has a cost, which the cell handles with its peroxidases.
1089: Two cysteines of the protein are linked by a disulfide bond. The enzyme PDI takes their electrons.
1090: The oxidised Cys-Gly-His-Cys active site swaps its disulfide with the thiols of the substrate (thiol-disulfide exchange). Reduced PDI can also correct mispaired bonds (isomerisation).
1091: What is the active-site motif of PDI?
1093: PDI is recharged by the enzyme Ero1, which passes the electrons to oxygen: hydrogen peroxide is formed.
1094: Ero1α re-oxidises PDI through a cysteine relay and its FAD, then reduces O₂ to H₂O₂. Peroxiredoxin 4 and the peroxidases GPx7/8 use this H₂O₂ to oxidise other PDIs.
1095: What is the final electron acceptor?
1099: From cisterna to cisterna, the sugar tree is pruned then rebuilt. Colours: GlcNAc dark blue, mannose green, galactose yellow, sialic acid purple.
1100: A high-mannose glycan has become a sialylated biantennary complex glycan, the signature of secreted proteins.
1102: In the cis-Golgi, three mannoses are removed: the tree is pruned before being rebuilt differently.
1103: MAN1A1, A2 and C1, specific for α1-2 linkages: Man₈ → Man₅GlcNAc₂. Inhibited by kifunensine. A glycan that stays at this stage is called “high-mannose”.
1104: Which linkages do mannosidases I cut?
1106: A first GlcNAc is added. Sugars arrive activated, carried by a nucleotide (here UDP).
1107: The step that commits to hybrid and complex glycans. Nucleotide sugars enter the Golgi through antiporters, in exchange for the UMP produced by hydrolysis of the released UDP.
1108: In what form is GlcNAc supplied?
1110: Two more mannoses are removed from the other branch.
1111: MAN2A1 acts only after GlcNAc-transferase I. It leaves the Man₃GlcNAc₂ core common to all N-glycans. Inhibited by swainsonine.
1117: A second GlcNAc caps the other branch: the glycan now has two antennae.
1118: Other transferases (MGAT4, MGAT5) can add a third and a fourth antenna, and FUT8 a fucose on the first GlcNAc of the core.
1124: In the trans-Golgi, a galactose is added at the tip of each antenna.
1125: B4GALT1, a Mn²⁺ enzyme: it forms the N-acetyllactosamine motif Galβ1-4GlcNAc.
1131: Finally a negatively charged sialic acid ends each antenna. The glycoprotein is mature.
1132: ST6GAL1 (α2-6 linkage) or ST3GAL (α2-3); the donor is CMP-sialic acid, the only nucleotide sugar with a single phosphate. Sialic acid masks the galactose: without it, the protein is captured by the hepatocyte asialoglycoprotein receptor.
1138: How the cell addresses its digestive enzymes to the lysosome: two reactions put a tag on their mannoses.
1139: Mannose-6-phosphate is recognised in the trans-Golgi network by its receptors, which carry the enzyme to endosomes.
1141: Enzymes bound for the lysosome receive a tag: a GlcNAc-phosphate is grafted onto one of their mannoses.
1142: The enzyme (GNPTAB/GNPTG) of the cis-Golgi recognises a surface patch of lysosomal hydrolases and transfers GlcNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc onto carbon 6 of a mannose. Its deficiency is mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease).
1143: Which disease results from its deficiency?
1148: The GlcNAc is removed: mannose-6-phosphate is unmasked. A receptor will carry it to endosomes, then the lysosome.
1149: Mannose-6-phosphate is bound at pH ≈ 6.5 by the receptors CI-MPR and CD-MPR, then released in the acidic endosome. This is the basis of enzyme replacement therapies for lysosomal diseases.
1150: Why does the receptor release the enzyme in the endosome?
1154: Ten reactions in the cytosol: one glucose is split into two pyruvates. Two ATP invested, four harvested.
1155: Glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pi + 2 NAD⁺ → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H₂O.
1156: Incoming glucose is phosphorylated at once: now charged, it can no longer leave the cell. Cost: one ATP.
1157: Hexokinase is inhibited by its product. In the hepatocyte, glucokinase (hexokinase IV) has a low affinity (≈ 8 mM), is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate and is sequestered in the nucleus by GKRP when fasting.
1158: Which form is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate?
1163: The six-membered ring is rearranged into a five-membered ring: glucose-6-phosphate becomes fructose-6-phosphate.
1164: Aldose–ketose isomerisation through an enediol intermediate, reversible.
1169: Second ATP invested: a second phosphate is added. This is the step that truly commits the sugar to glycolysis.
1170: The main control step: inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP and above all by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which PFK2 produces in the liver under insulin.
